items.q: How does a large message travel across the internet?
options: Split into packets, each stamped with source and destination IP, forwarded by routers
As an email attachment every time
Only over a single direct cable from sender to receiver
As one continuous unbroken stream that must stay together

explain.right: Data is chopped into addressed packets that routers forward hop by hop; they can even take different paths and arrive out of order.
explain.wrong: It isn't one indivisible stream or a single dedicated cable, and packets, not emails, are the unit of transfer.

items.q: When would UDP be a better fit than TCP?
options: A live video call, where speed matters more than resending a lost frame
Any time you want guaranteed, in-order delivery
Downloading a program where every byte must be correct

explain.right: UDP's fast, no-guarantee delivery suits live media/games, where a late or lost packet is better dropped than waited on.
explain.wrong: File downloads and statements need TCP's reliable, in-order delivery; guaranteed delivery is exactly what TCP (not UDP) provides.

options: It is the website's actual address
It translates a human-readable domain name into an IP address
It stores the web page's content

explain.right: DNS is the directory that turns a name like example.com into the IP address your computer then connects to.
explain.wrong: DNS is the lookup system, not the address itself (that's the IP), and it neither encrypts traffic nor hosts page content.

items.q: In HTTP, what does a status code like 404 represent?
options: Part of the server's response, indicating the outcome (here: not found)
The number of images on the page
The size of the page in kilobytes

explain.right: The server's response includes a status code (200 OK, 404 Not Found, 500 error) summarizing what happened with the request.
explain.wrong: It's not a size, an IP, or an image count; it's the response's outcome indicator.

items.q: Briefly trace what happens from typing https://example.com to seeing the page.
rubric: DNS resolves the domain name to an IP address
A connection is opened to that IP (TCP, plus TLS for HTTPS)
The browser sends an HTTP request and the server returns a response (HTML + status)
The browser parses the HTML, fetches additional resources (CSS/JS/images), and renders

explain.right: Good answers go DNS lookup -> TCP/TLS connection -> HTTP request/response -> parse and fetch sub-resources -> render.
explain.wrong: A weak answer says 'the browser just downloads the page' with no DNS, connection, request/response, or rendering steps.
